title: To what extent is ChatGPT useful for language teacher lesson plan creation?
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can be useful for generating foreign language lesson plans for teachers, and more specifically whether increasing prompt specificity changes the quality and consistency of the generated plans. The authors focus on the problem of generative AI variability and the possibility that AI-generated lesson plans may reflect outdated pedagogical practices rather than current research-based language teaching approaches.

The study uses ChatGPT-4 with a zero-shot prompting approach. Five prompts of increasing specificity were created for a high school Level I Spanish lesson on Costa Rican restaurants and were each entered into 10 separate chats, yielding 50 lesson plans. The lesson plans were scored against a rubric aligned with ACTFL-oriented lesson-planning criteria and edTPA-related expectations used in pre-service teacher preparation at the authors’ institution. The analysis compared scores, word counts, and output similarity across prompt versions.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT can generate reasonably strong lesson plans, but added specificity does not guarantee better outputs. The inclusion of a detailed lesson-plan template sometimes reduced alignment with the rubric, while providing a checklist of required criteria improved performance the most. The authors also found substantial variability across repeated outputs from the same prompt and identified recurring weaknesses, including inconsistent cultural connections and occasional reliance on older instructional patterns such as audio-lingual-style activities. The paper is primarily descriptive and cautionary, offering practical guidance for teachers and teacher educators on prompt design and the need to critically review AI-generated materials.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical descriptive study with a clear analytic workflow (50 ChatGPT outputs, rubric scoring, ANOVA, PERMANOVA, ANOSIM), but it is not a causal evaluation of student or teacher outcomes and has no comparison group beyond prompt variants. It is best classified as correlational/descriptive evidence about model behavior in a specific task context.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical usefulness for teacher lesson-plan drafting, but the demonstrated impact is limited to output quality and efficiency proxies rather than measured real-world gains. Any broader impact on K-12 practice remains indirect and modest because the study does not test implementation at scale or downstream educational outcomes.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT 4.0 used to generate foreign-language teacher lesson plans from zero-shot prompts, with prompts varied in specificity and structure to assess lesson-plan quality and variability.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was generally useful for drafting lesson plans, suggesting potential time-saving support for teachers. Across 50 generated lesson plans (5 prompts x 10 replicates), mean rubric scores were fairly high overall (e.g., 20.1/25 for P1 and 21.6/25 for P5), indicating the tool can produce workable plans with limited prompting, although quality was inconsistent.
finding.measure: Lesson-plan rubric score and word count for AI-generated lesson plans

finding.finding_summary: Increasing prompt specificity did not reliably improve lesson-plan quality and sometimes reduced it. Mean scores were not linear across prompts: P2 averaged 21.2/25, P3 dropped to 19.8/25 after adding a template, P4 remained at 19.6/25, and P5 rose to 21.6/25 when explicit criteria were added; the overall prompt-group difference was only marginal (ANOVA p=0.0442) and pairwise tests were not significant after correction.
finding.measure: Rubric-based lesson-plan scores across five prompt conditions

finding.finding_summary: The model showed substantial non-determinism: identical prompts often produced lesson plans differing by at least five rubric elements, and scores ranged widely within prompt groups (e.g., P1 from 16/25 to 23/25; P5 from 20/25 to 25/25). Distance analyses and hierarchical clustering showed some separation by prompt, but also many cases where outputs from different prompt types converged, underscoring inconsistent performance for lesson-plan generation.
finding.measure: Within-prompt variability in rubric scores; Jaccard dissimilarity; NMDS/PERMANOVA/ANOSIM clustering of prompt outputs
